name: Figure skating
energy: A free skate of about 4 min is roughly three quarters aerobic, with the rest from short explosive jumps, spins and footwork.
summary: Figure skating needs explosive take-offs, fast rotation and single-leg landings of up to 9 times body weight, and the knee, ankle and foot carry most injuries. The plan builds leg power and landing capacity, a stiff rotating trunk, tendon and ankle robustness, and keeps energy intake high enough to protect bone.

evidence.claim: Ankle sprain is the most common injury, patellar tendinopathy the most common overuse injury, and stress fractures the most common overuse injury in female singles; pairs accounts for most upper-limb injuries.
Jump landing impact rises with extra revolutions, from about 3 to 9 times body weight.
evidence.source: Lockwood, Baudin & Gervais, citing Lockwood & Gervais 1995

evidence.claim: Free skating was estimated at about 74% aerobic, 12% anaerobic lactic and 14% anaerobic alactic, with peak HR about 194 bpm and lactate about 9.7 mmol/L.
evidence.source: ECSS 2012 congress abstract, energetic demand profile in figure skating

variants.name: Singles
variants.desc: The most jumps and the most overuse injuries, including stress fractures in female singles.
variants.note: Most jump power and landing work, plus careful jump-count and energy-intake rules.

variants.name: Pairs
variants.desc: Lifts, twists and throws: men lift a partner overhead, women land throws and hold positions in the air.
variants.note: Men add overhead pressing and shoulder work; women keep the singles landing work and add trunk and shoulder stability.

variants.name: Ice dance
variants.desc: No multi-revolution jumps; deep edges, footwork, lifts and longer continuous effort.
variants.note: Fewer jumps, more single-leg strength, edge-control hip work and aerobic conditioning; men add lift strength.

off.name: Lower strength and jump power
off.focus: Leg strength and vertical take-off power.

slots.note: Land quietly on two feet; full rest.
Stick the landing on one leg, like a jump landing.

off.name: Rotation and single-leg control
off.focus: Fast rotation, a stiff trunk and landing-leg strength.

slots.note: Both directions, even though you jump one way.
Isometric holds for the patellar tendon.

off.name: Upper body, back and ankles
off.focus: Upper strength for arms and lifts, lumbar capacity and lower leg.

slots.note: Pairs men: progress overhead pressing here.

pre.name: Rotation, upper and tendons
pre.focus: Rotational speed, lift strength and lower-leg capacity.

in.name: Competition season strength
in.focus: Hold strength and power in 30 minutes.

in.name: Rotation and protection
in.focus: Short session up to 3 days before a competition.

off.name: Aerobic base
off.why: About three quarters of a free skate is aerobic; a low-impact base spares the landing leg.

pre.name: Programme-length intervals
pre.work: 4 x 4 min with 10 s sprints every 40 s
pre.intensity: Hard but steady with all-out bursts
pre.why: Matches a 4 min free skate with jumps inside it (practice).

tests.name: Countermovement jump
tests.how: Hands on hips, jump mat or My Jump app, best of 3.
tests.note: No verified skating norms; practice bands for adult men, women about 20% lower, juniors lower still. Track change.

tests.name: Single-leg hop for distance
tests.how: Hop and stick on each leg, best of 3; record the difference between legs.
tests.note: Landing leg and take-off leg differ; flag gaps over 10-15% (practice).

tests.name: Y-balance anterior reach
tests.how: Single-leg stance, reach forward along a tape line with the other foot; best of 3 each side.
tests.note: A difference over 4 cm is linked to lower-limb injury in other sports (Plisky 2006).

tests.name: Side plank hold
tests.how: Forearm side plank, straight line from head to heel, held to failure each side.
tests.note: Practice bands; track left-right balance, which matters for one-way rotation.

week: Competition weekend: heavy lower session Monday or Tuesday.
Rotation and protection session Wednesday at the latest.
Keep jump-heavy on-ice sessions away from the day after heavy lifting where possible.
No heavy lower work within 72 h of competing.
Day after competing: easy bike or swim and mobility.
primer: 2 x 2 off-ice half or single turn jumps each way
1 x 3 single-leg hop and stick each side

lines: Last heavy lower lift 5-7 days before competing.
Gym volume down about 50%, keep the load.
Cut total jump count, keep full run-throughs sharp.
Keep eating normally; do not diet into a competition.

rules: Never restrict food to stay light; skipped meals and low energy intake are linked to injury and stress fractures.
Bone pain in the shin, foot or lower back that worsens with jumping: stop jumping and see a doctor.
Build jump counts gradually after any break.
Check boot fit each season and after growth spurts.
Under 16: no depth jumps and no 1RM testing; technique-led lifting.
Train rotation both ways in the gym even though you jump one way.
